modern_osis:
Original heading

David's numbering the people.

David's census and the place of the temple

Chronicles does not recount David's sin concerning Uriah or the troubles that followed it; those events were not necessary to the particular subjects being addressed here.

But this book does recount David's sin in numbering the people.

The atonement made for that sin revealed the place where the temple would be built.

God's command that David build an altar was a blessed sign of reconciliation.

The Lord also showed that he accepted David's offerings on that altar.

This points to Christ, who was made sin and a curse for us.

The Lord was pleased to crush him so that through him God might be, not a consuming fire against us, but a God reconciled to us.

It is good to continue attending the ordinances in which we have already experienced signs of God's presence and discovered that he truly is with us.

We can say, “God graciously met me here; therefore I will continue to expect to meet him here.”
classic_reading:
[1Chr.21.1]
Chapter 21
David's numbering the people.
--No mention is made in this book of David's sin in the matter of Uriah, neither of the troubles that followed it: they had no needful connexion with the subjects here noted. But David's sin, in numbering the people, is related: in the atonement made for that sin, there was notice of the place on which the temple should be built. The command to David to build an altar, was a blessed token of reconciliation. God testified his acceptance of David's offerings on this altar. Thus Christ was made sin, and a curse for us; it pleased the Lord to bruise him, that through him, God might be to us, not a consuming Fire, but a reconciled God. It is good to continue attendance on those ordinances in which we have experienced the tokens of God's presence, and have found that he is with us of a truth. Here God graciously met me, therefore I will still expect to meet him.

David prepares to build the temple (verses 1–5)

After the terrible judgment upon Israel for David's sin, God showed him where the temple should be built.

David was therefore moved to make preparations for this great work.

Although David was not to build it himself, he would do everything he could.

Before his death, he made abundant preparations.

Whatever our hands can do for God, our souls and the people around us, let us do with all our strength while life remains. After death there is no more work or planning.

When the Lord does not employ us in the role we hoped for, we should not become discouraged or idle.

We should do all we can, even in a humbler sphere.

David instructs Solomon (verses 6–16)

David gave Solomon three reasons for building the temple.

First, God had appointed Solomon. Nothing more strongly encourages service than knowing the Lord has assigned it to us.

Second, Solomon would have the peace and opportunity to complete it. When God gives rest, he expects us to use it for work.

Third, God had promised to establish Solomon's kingdom. God's gracious promises should strengthen and encourage our service.

David explained how much he had already prepared.

He was not boasting; he wanted Solomon to enter the work cheerfully.

Solomon should never imagine that constructing a temple would give him permission to sin.

On the contrary, the work would not be acceptable if he failed to obey God's commands.

In both spiritual service and spiritual conflict, we need courage and determination.

Others are instructed to help (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 17–19</reference>)

Anything done to make God's word more widely known and obeyed is like contributing a stone or a bar of gold to the temple's construction.

That should encourage people distressed by seeing so little fruit from their efforts.

Much good may appear after our death that we never expected.

Let us not grow weary of doing good.

The work belongs to the Prince of Peace.

He begins and completes it, and graciously employs us as his instruments.

Therefore, let us rise and work, encouraging and helping one another.

Let us follow his rule and example, depend upon his grace and remain assured that our work in the Lord will not be wasted.

Verses 1-5
On occasion of the terrible judgment inflicted on Israel for the sin of David, God pointed out the place where he would have the temple built; upon which, David was excited to make preparations for the great work. David must not build, but he would do all he could; he prepared abundantly before his death. What our hands find to do for God, and our souls, and those round us, let us do it with all our might, before our death; for after death there is no device nor working. And when the Lord refuses to employ us in those services which we desired, we must not be discouraged or idle, but do what we can, though in a humbler sphere.
[1Chr.22.6-1Chr.22.16]
Verses 6-16
David gives Solomon the reason why he should build the temple. Because God named him. Nothing is more powerful to engage us in any service for God, than to know that we are appointed thereto. Because he would have leisure and opportunity to do it. He should have peace and quietness. Where God gives rest, he expects work. Because God had promised to establish his kingdom. God's gracious promises should quicken and strengthen our religious service. David delivered to Solomon an account of the vast preparations he had made for this building; not from pride and vain-glory, but to encourage Solomon to engage cheerfully in the great work. He must not think, by building the temple, to purchase a dispensation to sin; on the contrary, his doing that would not be accepted, if he did not take heed to fulfil the statutes of the Lord. In our spiritual work, as well as in our spiritual warfare, we have need of courage and resolution. ( [1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19] 1Ch 22:17-19)
[1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19]
Verses 17-19
Whatever is done towards rendering the word of God generally known and attended to, is like bringing a stone, or an ingot of gold, towards erecting the temple. This should encourage us when we grieve that we do not see more fruit of our labours; much good may appear after our death, which we never thought of. Let us not then be weary of well doing. The work is in the hands of the Prince of peace. As he, the Author and Finisher of the work, is pleased to employ us as his instruments, let us arise and be doing, encouraging and helping one another; working by his rule, after his example, in dependence on his grace, assured that he will be with us, and that our labour shall not be in vain in the Lord.

Solomon's succession and temple service (verses 1–23)

After giving instructions about the temple's construction, David organized its service and appointed the officers responsible.

When members of the same family work together in God's service, it should encourage them to love and assist one another.

The Levites' work (verses 24–32)

The population of Israel had grown, and more workers were needed in the temple.

Every Israelite arriving with an offering should find a Levite ready to help.

When there is more work to do, it is fitting to have more workers.

The great difference between a true Christian and other people is a new heart and a spiritual mind.

A person with such a heart takes great delight in God's commandments and finds refreshment in his appointed worship.

For a spiritual person, every form of service brings satisfaction.

Such a person wants to abound continually in the Lord's work and is happiest serving so good a Master in so pleasant a task.

It does not matter whether the person is called to lead or to serve under someone else's leadership.

May we seek the Lord and serve him sincerely, trusting his word and leaving everything else to his wise disposal.

Verses 24-32

When more work is to be done, it is pity but there should be more workmen. A new heart, a spiritual mind, which delights greatly in God's commandments, and can find a refreshing feast in his ordinances, forms the great distinction between the true Christian and all other men in the world. To the spiritual man every service will yield satisfaction. He will be ever abounding in the work of the Lord; being never so happy as when employed for such a good Master, in so pleasant a service. He will not regard whether he is called to take the lead, or to keep the charge of others who are placed over him. May we seek and serve the Lord uprightly, and leave all the rest to his disposal, by faith in his word.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The divisions of the priests and Levites.

The priests and Levites receive their duties

When everyone has a place, understands the work assigned to it and carries out that work faithfully, having more people involved is a blessing.

In Christ's mystical body, every member contributes something useful to the good of the whole.

Christ is the High Priest over God's house.

All believers have been made priests, yet they are to submit to him.

In Christ there is no difference in spiritual acceptance between bond and free, or between older and younger.

Younger brothers and sisters, if sincere and faithful, are no less acceptable to Christ than their elders.

May we all be children of the Lord, prepared to sing his praises forever in the heavenly temple.

The divisions of the priests and Levites.
--When every one has, knows, and keeps his place and work, the more there are the better. In the mystical body of Christ, every member has its use, for the good of the whole. Christ is High Priest over the house of God, to whom all believers, being made priests, are to be in subjection. In Christ, no difference is made between bond and free, elder and younger. The younger brethren, if faithful and sincere, shall be no less acceptable to Christ than the fathers. May we all be children of the Lord, fitted to sing his praises for ever in his temple above.

Original heading

The singers and musicians.

The musicians appointed to worship

David organized those appointed to sing and play music in the temple.

Here, to prophesy means to praise God with great earnestness and devout affection under the influence of the Holy Spirit.

Poetry and music were used to awaken these affections.

But unless the Spirit of God brings life and fervor into our worship, even the most carefully ordered services remain lifeless and worthless forms.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.25.1]

The singers and musicians.
--David put those in order who were appointed to be singers and musicians in the temple. To prophesy, in this place, means praising God with great earnestness and devout affections, under the influences of the Holy Spirit. In raising these affections, poetry and music were employed. If the Spirit of God do not put life and fervour into our devotions, they will, however ordered, be a lifeless, worthless form.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The offices of the Levites.

The Levites' duties and the temple treasury

The temple's gatekeepers and treasurers needed strength and courage. They had to prevent unauthorized entry into the sanctuary and protect its sacred treasures.

Each day the altar consumed considerable supplies: flour, wine, oil, salt and fuel. The lamps also needed provisions.

Stores of these items were kept ready, together with the sacred clothing and utensils.

These were the treasures of God's house.

They pictured the abundance available in our heavenly Father's house, where there is more than enough for all.

From the unsearchable riches of Christ, pictured by those treasuries, our needs are supplied.

Having received from his fullness, we should give him all the glory and use our abilities and possessions according to his will.

The chapter also records officials and judges.

Civil government, like the ministry of God's word, is an ordinance of God for the good of his church and must not be neglected.

The Levites who served directly in the sanctuary, the singers and the gatekeepers were not also assigned this outward administrative work. Each responsibility already required their full attention.

Whatever our position, we need wisdom, courage, strong faith, holy affections and steadfastness in doing our duty.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.26.1]
Chapter 26
The offices of the Levites.
--The porters and treasurers of the temple, had occasion for strength and valour to oppose those who wrongly attempted to enter the sanctuary, and to guard the sacred treasures. Much was expended daily upon the altar; flour, wine, oil, salt, fuel, beside the lamps; quantities of these were kept beforehand, besides the sacred vestments and utensils. These were the treasures of the house of God. These treasures typified the plenty there is in our heavenly Father's house, enough and to spare. From those sacred treasuries, the unsearchable riches of Christ, all our wants are supplied; and receiving from his fulness, we must give him the glory, and endeavour to dispose of our abilities and substance according to his will. We have an account of those employed as officers and judges. The magistracy is an ordinance of God for the good of the church, as truly as the ministry, and must not be neglected. None of the Levites who were employed in the service of the sanctuary, none of the singers or porters, were concerned in this outward business; one duty was enough to engage the whole man. Wisdom, courage, strength of faith, holy affections, and constancy of mind in doing our duty, are requisite or useful for every station.

David's military organization (verses 1–15)

In earthly kingdoms, being prepared for war helps preserve peace.

In the same way, nothing encourages Satan's attacks more than spiritual carelessness.

As long as we stand equipped with the whole armor of God, exercising faith and keeping our hearts ready for the struggle, we will certainly be secure and probably also enjoy peace within.

The rulers and officers (verses 16–34)

David's officers were responsible for managing the fields, vineyards, herds and flocks that formed the wealth of kings in that part of the world.

The wisdom of rulers is often shown by their choice of ministers and officials.

Ordinary people show wisdom in choosing advisers as well.

Yet with all these counselors around him, David preferred God's word above them all.

“Your testimonies are my delight and my counselors.”

David calls Israel and Solomon to know and serve God (verses 1–10)

During David's last illness, many of the leading priests and Levites were in Jerusalem.

When he found himself able to speak, David recalled his desire to build the temple, God's refusal of that plan, and the gracious purpose God had for Solomon.

He called them to remain steadfast in their duty and faithfulness to the Lord.

We cannot do our work properly without resolution and strength received from God's grace.

True religion has two distinct parts: knowing God and worshiping God.

David called Solomon to know the God of his father and serve him with a whole heart and willing mind.

God makes himself known through his works and his word.

Only divine revelation fully reveals his character: his providence, holy law, judgment on sinners, blessed gospel and the Spirit's work in all genuine believers.

A person governed only by natural human thinking cannot receive this knowledge.

But through God's revelation, we understand the worth of the Savior's atonement and the Spirit's sanctifying work, which move us to obey his commandments.

The sinner then takes the proper place at the foot of the cross, acknowledging guilt, helplessness and deserved judgment while expecting all necessary gifts from the free mercy and grace of God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Having been forgiven much, the repentant sinner learns to love much.

David gives Solomon the temple plan (verses 11–21)

The temple was sacred and pointed toward Christ.

Its form had to be directed by God.

Christ is the true temple, the church is the gospel temple, and heaven is the everlasting temple.

All are established according to God's wise and eternal purpose for his glory and our good.

David gave Solomon the design so that he would follow God's rule.

He also prepared costly materials and utensils.

Then David encouraged Solomon to look to God first for help.

Do not be discouraged: the Lord will help you.

The God who cared for our fathers and enabled them to complete the service entrusted to their generation will not leave us while he still has work to accomplish in us or through us.

Good work prospers when everyone involved sincerely supports it.

Let us hope in God's mercy: if we seek him, he will be found by us.

Chapter 28
Chapter Outline
David exhorts the people to the fear of the Lord. | (1-10) |
He gives instructions for the temple. | (11-21) |
Verses 1-10
During David's last sickness, many chief priests and Levites were at Jerusalem. Finding himself able, David spoke of his purpose to build a temple for God, and of God's disallowing that purpose. He opened to them God's gracious purposes concerning Solomon. David charged them to cleave stedfastly to God and their duty. We cannot do our work as we should, unless we put on resolution, and fetch in strength from Divine grace. Religion or piety has two distinct parts. The first is knowledge of God, the second is worship of God. David says, Know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing mind. God is made known by his works and word. Revelation alone shows the whole character of God, in his providence, his holy law, his condemnation of sinners, his blessed gospel, and the ministration of the Spirit to all true believers. The natural man cannot receive this knowledge of God. But thus we learn the value of the Saviour's atonement, and of the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, and are influenced to walk in all his commandments. It brings a sinner to his proper place at the foot of the cross, as a poor, guilty, helpless worm, deserving wrath, yet expecting every thing needful from the free mercy and grace of God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Having been forgiven much, the pardoned sinner learns to love much.
[1Chr.28.11-1Chr.28.21]
Verses 11-21
The temple must be a sacred thing, and a type of Christ; it must be framed by Divine teaching. Christ is the true temple, the church is the gospel temple, and heaven the everlasting temple; all are framed according to the Divine counsels, and the plan laid in the Divine wisdom, ordained before the world, for God's glory and our good. David gave this pattern to Solomon, that he might go by rule. Materials were provided for the most costly utensils of the temple. Directions were given which way to look for help in this great undertaking. Be not dismayed; God will help thee, and thou must look up to him in the first place. We may be sure that God, who owned our fathers, and carried them through the services of their day, will, in like manner, never leave us, while he has any work to do in us, or by us. Good work is likely to go on, when all concerned are hearty in furthering it. Let us hope in God's mercy; if we seek him, he will be found of us.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid induces the princes and people to offer willingly.1–9His thanksgiving and prayer.10–19Solomon enthroned.20–25David's reign and death.26–30
David and the people give willingly (verses 1–9)

Works of devotion and charity should be carried out willingly, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

David led by his example.

He gave not because he had to or because he wanted to impress people.

He gave because his heart was devoted to God's house, and he believed he could never do too much to advance the good work.

Those who want to encourage others toward good must take the lead themselves.

David's prayer of thanksgiving (verses 10–19)

We can scarcely imagine the grandeur of the temple and its surrounding buildings, made with so much gold and silver.

Yet Christ's unsearchable riches surpass the temple's splendor infinitely more than the temple itself surpassed the humblest cottage.

Instead of boasting about their generous gifts, David gave solemn thanks to the Lord.

Everything they offered for God's temple already belonged to him.

Had they tried to keep it all, death would soon have taken it from them.

The only way to use it for their true advantage was to dedicate it to the service of the One who had given it.

Solomon is enthroned (verses 20–25)

The entire assembly joined David in worshiping God.

Whoever leads the congregation in prayer, only those who join sincerely benefit.

It is not primarily a matter of bowing the head but lifting up the soul.

Solomon sat upon the Lord's throne.

His kingdom was a type of the kingdom of the Messiah, whose throne is truly the Lord's.

David's reign and death (verses 26–30)

After reading 2 Samuel, we might hardly have expected David to appear so honorable at the end of his life.

Yet his repentance had been as remarkable as his sin.

His patient conduct through suffering and during his final years seems to have had a good effect on the people around him.

Blessed be God: even the greatest sinners may hope for a glorious departure when they repent and flee to the atoning blood of the Savior.

Notice the difference between David, the man after God's own heart, as he lived and died, and false professors who imitate only his sins and use his failures as excuses for their own crimes.

Let us watch and pray, lest temptation overcome us and sin dishonor God and wound our consciences.

When we recognize that we have offended him, may we imitate David's repentance and patience, looking forward to a glorious resurrection through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Verses 1-9
What is done in works of piety and charity, should be done willingly, not by constraint; for God loves a cheerful giver. David set a good example. This David offered, not from constraint, or for show; but because he had set his affection to the house of God, and thought he could never do enough towards promoting that good work. Those who would draw others to good, must lead the way themselves.
[1Chr.29.10-1Chr.29.19]
Verses 10-19
We cannot form a right idea of the magnificence of the temple, and the buildings around it, about which such quantities of gold and silver were employed. But the unsearchable riches of Christ exceed the splendour of the temple, infinitely more than that surpassed the meanest cottage on earth. Instead of boasting of these large oblations, David gave solemn thanks to the Lord. All they gave for the Lord's temple was his own; if they attempted to keep it, death would soon have removed them from it. The only use they could make of it to their real advantage, was, to consecrate it to the service of Him who gave it.
[1Chr.29.20-1Chr.29.25]
Verses 20-25
This great assembly joined with David in adoring God. Whoever is the mouth of the congregation, those only have the benefit who join him, not by bowing down the head, so much as by lifting up the soul. Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord. Solomon's kingdom typified the kingdom of the Messiah, whose throne is the throne of the Lord.
[1Chr.29.26-1Chr.29.30]
Verses 26-30
When we read the second book of Samuel, we could scarcely have expected to behold David appear so illustrious in his closing scene. But his repentance had been as remarkable as his sin; and his conduct during his afflictions, and towards the end of his life, appears to have had a good effect on his subjects. Blessed be God, even the chief of sinners may hope for a glorious departure, when brought to repent and flee for refuge to the Saviour's atoning blood. Let us mark the difference between the spirit and character of the man after God's own heart, living and dying, and those of worthless professors, who resemble him in nothing but their sins, and who wickedly try to excuse their crimes by his sins. Let us watch and pray, lest we be overcome by temptation, and overtaken by sin, to the dishonour of God, and the wounding of our own consciences. When we feel that we have offended, let us follow David's example of repentance and patience, looking for a glorious resurrection, through our Lord Jesus Christ.
